Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Psychiatrist
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Avoid Sex: Sex, Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Sara, 58, an Oceania-born psychiatrist with a diverse background, has been struggling to manage her life since a life-threatening accident nearly two years ago. The traumatic event that still haunts her occurred during one of her daily commutes; she was hit by another car while crossing the street near her office building in downtown Los Angeles. The sudden collision left her shaken and in severe pain, but also triggered a series of intrusive thoughts about the trauma that have never fully subsided. Since the accident, Sara has been plagued by unwanted memories that surface at unexpected moments. Her daily routine as a psychiatrist is often interrupted by vivid flashbacks where she relives the moment of impact, feeling the jarring sensation and overwhelming fear all over again. The images of cars hitting each other now serve as potent triggers for her distress. These intrusive thoughts are especially troubling when she walks near intersections or sees vehicles moving at high speeds on the highway. In an effort to manage these intense emotions, Sara has adopted a strict regimen of controlling her feelings. She avoids situations that might trigger strong emotional reactions and often isolates herself from social interactions. This includes avoiding sex, which she now associates with vulnerability and heightened emotionality, and even going to sleep at night because lying in the dark can evoke sensations reminiscent of those during the accident. Her avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on her personal life; after being divorced for several years, Sara has found it increasingly difficult to reconnect with others, fearing that any intimate relationship might bring up unwanted memories and feelings. Sara's startle response is also quite pronounced; she often feels jumpy or easily startled by sudden noises or movements. Her sense of safety is deeply compromised, leading her to adopt unusual behaviors like keeping her back against walls where she can see the room clearly, as if this position will somehow protect her from unforeseen dangers. At night, Sara wakes up frequently, driven by an overwhelming need to check whether she is safe, convinced that some residual threat lurks in the dark. The memory of the accident itself remains fragmented and confusing. Sara has trouble recalling a coherent sequence of events; she can’t put together a clear narrative of what happened, even to herself. Sometimes, certain details or sensations trigger the full memory without warning, leaving her disoriented and anxious. This confusion about the timeline adds another layer of distress, as she questions whether she fully understands or processed the trauma. Sara has come to believe that this accident has permanently changed her for the worse. She harbors self-doubt about her ability to make sound decisions and often second-guesses herself in both professional and personal contexts. Her world view has also shifted; Sara now perceives the world as an inherently dangerous place, a perspective that colors how she approaches daily life. Despite her efforts to maintain control over her emotions and avoid triggering situations, Sara’s symptoms have gradually worsened over time. The cumulative effect of these coping strategies has left her feeling isolated and increasingly disconnected from her colleagues and patients at work. Her professional interactions are strained, as she finds it challenging to engage fully with others without the fear of being triggered. What finally brought Sara to seek help was a recent incident where she had a panic attack during a meeting with a patient, unable to control the intrusive thoughts that flooded her mind. This episode was particularly distressing for her because it highlighted how much her ability to work effectively had diminished. She is most afraid of losing her professional identity and being unable to continue practicing as a psychiatrist, but at the same time, she hopes that through therapy, she can regain some sense of control over her life and begin to heal from this traumatic event.
